newsitem.title: FINLAND: Mobiles fraud a nuisance, no loss -Nokia.
newsitem.headline: Mobiles fraud a nuisance, no loss -Nokia.

text.p: Finnish telecoms group Nokia Oy does not expect to incur losses from illegal tampering with mobile phones made by the company, but the affair could be a time-consuming nuisance, a Nokia spokesman said on Thursday.

"We mobile-phone makers are bystanders," said Nokia Mobile Phones head of information Lauri Kivinen after Finnish police said they had found a number of mobile phones, most made by Nokia, with network identification codes illegally changed.
"It is our opinion that we will not incur any financial losses," he said by telephone. "But this will be a nuisance."

Cellular handsets sold by Nokia and other manufacturers to wholesalers and retailers have an IMEI (international mobile station equipment identity) code used to identify the handset in the network of a telecoms operator, Kivinen said.
Some operators, aiming to acquire quickly a great number of users to fill their network's capacity, offer customers mobile handsets at big discounts hoping to reap profit from use fees.

Finnish police found that mobile phones apparently bought abroad at such discounts had had their IMEI codes changed to fit Finnish networks and been sold at current market prices to ordinary customers.
The scam was unveiled when permission was cancelled to use one mobile phone in a domestic network by closing its IMEI code.
Several other mobile phones also suddenly went dead and police found that the handsets that had been tampered with had all been re-equipped with the same IMEI code.
"Cloned (mobile) phones have been distributed for retailing for about a year, apparently in great numbers," daily Helsingin Sanomat on Thursday quoted a police officer as saying.
Kivinen said Nokia could not be held responsible because the manufacturer's guarantee was valid only for the original product, not for those that had been tampered with.
"It is unfortunate for all those innocent people which have fallen victim to this," he said.
The affair might lead people to consider where they buy their mobile handsets, he said. Some retailers are authorised by the product manufacturer.
"I don't think it will dent sales," he said when asked whether the scam, the full scope of which was not yet clear, could make potential new mobile phone users hesitate.
